utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, will you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager for today is Mr. Hasan Younis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber wishes to greet all those present, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, and Madam Registrar, who is assisting us today, and we also welcome the case manager for the Prosecution. Today we are going to hear a witness, but we first have to let the parties know before we begin with the hearing how we intend to proceed on Tuesday and Wednesday when we'll be discussing documents, so that those two hearing days will be useful and will allow the Judges to make appropriate rulings regarding the admission of documents. The Chamber wishes to thank both the Prosecution and the Defence attorneys for their filings regarding documents, indicating the origin of documents, the numbering of the documents; and the Defence also presented their detailed objections with respect to documents one by one, which means that these documents which are voluminous, coming from both parties, will allow us to properly rule regarding the admission of documents. These two hearings will proceed as follows and will be devoted to five different subjects: On each of the topics that I'm going to mention, the Prosecution and the Defence will express their opinions. The Prosecution will begin. They will elaborate on the topic that I'm going to indicate in a moment. Then the Defence counsel, both of them, will express their point of view. If necessary, the Prosecution will respond. And, of course, the Judges will put any questions they consider necessary to the parties. The topics are the following -- and the first topic, we believe that Tuesday should be devoted to the three first topics and Wednesday to the last two. The first three topics are the following: The first has to do with the sources and origin of the documents. I'll come back to that. The second topic will relate to technical problems related to documents. And the third topic will have to do with the relevance of documents. The fourth topic, which will be addressed on Wednesday, will have to do with questions related to 89(D). And the fifth topic will have to do with the documents which have to be admitted only through witness testimony. Regarding the topic of origin and source of documents and various questions linked to authenticity. Regarding the origin of those documents, in the columns "Sources and additional sources," the Chamber notes that several sources or origins of documents are mentioned, and I quote them: Sarajevo, the ABiH archives; the Zagreb archives; no source for some documents. There's 353 and 409; 16B Sarajevo Blaskic "Defence exhibit, witness Radic or Williams"; Sarajevo, 7th Brigade, Zenica archives; no source of information for 114. Then there are documents without stamps obtained from Vidovic. 280, it says "Kordic Defence team." There's also 282 indicated as Defence exhibit. For 312, 320, it is indicated they were obtained from the BiH Federation. We have to know what that means. 352 comes from the Bosnian government. 512, from the Croatian Embassy in The Hague. 392, Ivan Josipovic. Exhibits 392 to 97 were obtained from the Bosnian government. The Travnik prosecutor produces 393, 394, and 395. Then there is 398, 99, 401 coming from the law foundation; 403, coming from the Croatian Television; 406 is Miskovic; 407, from a Dutch officer who worked on the crime sites; 408 is a video recording made by an officer; 411, Dikic; 420, 21, coming from Zenica; 454 and 456, Team 9, a crime mission site; 467, coming from the Defence Ministry of BiH; 468 and on, from the RBiH Collection; 413 and 414, OTPD.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the President please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: There are several documents whose number has not been indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I'm going very quickly, I see it is difficult to follow me. And I am indicating that Amnesty International is mentioned for 479. 481 to 486 -- then there's one coming from the crime committee in Zenica, 582. Then there are documents that could perhaps be introduced now, 593, 594, 598. Regarding all these documents and the sources indicated, before taking a decision on their admissibility, the Chamber wishes to learn from the Prosecution how those documents came to -- into their possession coming from this same source. By way of example, how Amnesty International sent this document, which appears as 479. Was it on the basis of a written request from the Prosecution? Was it Amnesty International itself that sent this to the Prosecution? We would like to know for all the documents in what way those documents came to be in the possession of the OTP. If it was within the framework of an inquiry or investigation, how this happened; did the investigators go to the archives in Sarajevo or -- and made photocopies of those documents. Anyway, we would like to know simply in technical terms how those documents came to be in the possession of the Prosecutor. Also, the Chamber has noted on several occasions and specifically yesterday that documents and orders coming from BiH were produced by the Defence, whereas the Prosecution did not have them in their possession. So how is it possible that if the BiH archives documents were communicated to the OTP, the Defence has other documents which come from the same archives and which the Prosecution does not have? So we would like to know why the Defence has documents which the Prosecution does not, because in the case of an investigation into an archives, the whole archives is taken. And if some are left aside, those may be the ones that the Defence picked up. So we would like to know how is it that Defence produced documents which normally should have been in the possession of the Prosecution. And the Chamber believes that in future cross-examinations they might produce documents in support of questions put within the framework of the cross-examination of General Reinhardt, for instance, and those documents will come from the BiH army, whereas they should have been in the possession of the Prosecution. So regarding all the elements that I have indicated - the Sarajevo archives, Zagreb archives, open sources, unknown sources - the Chamber will next Tuesday request from the Prosecution that it gives us specific explanations under which conditions it obtained those documents, on what date, the way in which the documents were transmitted, and to tell us also if they can why orders which were in the ABiH archives, original orders, were not produced in the original, that we only have copies. There's a mystery there too which we need to clarify. Was it the archives services in Sarajevo which refused to give you originals, or do you have originals which you copied and then you sent back the originals? We need to be informed about this, because if we have originals in front of us, some discussions that took place or that will take place could have been avoided if we had the original documents. So we need such additional explanations from the Prosecution. Furthermore, concerning these documents, as I have said, we need to be informed how those documents were collected. I have discovered that the Croatian Embassy in The Hague has produced a document; there, too, we need to know was it the Prosecution who addressed the ambassador or the ambassador who sent the document to the Prosecution. We need to know the origin of that document. Regarding documents coming from the government, was it on the basis of a written request from the Prosecutor or was it a spontaneous contact from the government? So as far as possible, we would like to have these matters clarified, as we consider them to be very important. Regarding the authenticity of documents, to the extent to which the Prosecution is tendering certain documents into evidence, it is because the Prosecution believes that those documents are authentic. The Prosecution has been able to see that in the filings of the Defence authenticity is being contested. So in the light of the remarks made by the Defence, the Prosecution needs to tell us on what basis they believe these documents are authentic. Regarding military orders, there are a dozen or so which come from various sources, either from the BiH army or the HVO. The Chamber would like to know what are -- what were the procedures applied by the Prosecution with the BiH army regarding the diffusion of those documents. We have noted on several occasions that documents beared -- carried the name of the addressee to the 312th Unit, to the 7th Brigade, et cetera. Sometimes there was an addressee and in other cases there were orders with no addressees. There's an order, but we don't know who it is addressed to. So it would be desirable -- to the extent that the Prosecution is able to do that, of course, because it is up to them; they should have done this work in advance; and that is, to indicate to the Chamber what were the procedures that their investigators applied regarding these orders from the BiH army and the HVO, how they were issued, they're oral orders, written orders, the nature of those written orders, and how they were distributed, if the Prosecution is able to tell us. They may not be able to. But if they are, they should tell us that as they're asking for an order to be admitted and this is being challenged, that they should explain how those orders were taken, made by the BiH army. And then the Defence will tell us their point of view. So that is the first topic. On the basis of what I have said, the Prosecution will present to us all these elements; upon which we shall give the floor to the Defence, which will convey their views. That is the first topic. The second topic relates to technical problems linked to documents. We have noted on several occasions that documents were poorly photocopied and again, questions arise. If an investigator of the OTP photocopies a document, if he copies the original, how is it that on copies that we have seen there are areas that are blackened out and that are illegible? So these are important questions. If the Prosecution could explain to us why documents were badly photocopied, we will be glad to receive such information. We have also noted that some documents lack signatures. When it comes to military orders, it says "Commander," for instance, and a name, but no signature. So several questions arise: Was this document signed at a given point? Was it not signed? Was it a duplicate of an original? Because as you know, in the administration of countries, there's one document and then there are duplicates. The first document is signed by the author and the duplicates are not signed. So the question relating to documents without signatures is whether those documents are perhaps duplicates, which would explain why there's no signature on them. The Prosecution perhaps could provide us with some explanations in that regard. There's also contestations by the Defence regarding illegible signatures. By way of example, there was a document which could be attributed to the late Mr. Alagic, and there's a signature on it. In theory, Mr. Alagic must have signed other documents as well, and the Prosecution surely has in its possession Mr. Alagic's signature, and then it is quite easy to say, "This signature, which is being contested," and compare it with Mr. Alagic's signature appearing on such-and-such a document. Therefore, illegible signatures could be dealt with in that way. Then there are also documents which are written in hand and which appear in the binders which you have provided us with. These handwritten documents, one has to know again who wrote them, to what extent those handwritten documents were in the archives. There's a whole series of questions regarding handwritten documents. Perhaps the Prosecution can enlighten us on this. Also, sometimes documents in B/C/S have English translations but the English translations appear to be incomplete. Then again, if there are incomplete translations, why is that so? What is the reason? So there's a whole list of technical problems that have been raised, and the Defence has referred to them in their filings, and it would be desirable for the Prosecution to clarify these problems next Tuesday. The third topic, relevance, which is an important problem, as you well know. The Defence in conformity with the oral ruling of the Chamber has indicated in its filings the grounds for which they consider some documents not to be relevant, but we don't know more than that. It's just indicated that they are not relevant. If the Prosecution wishes to have all those documents tendered, it is because they consider them to be relevant; however, the Defence says that some of them are not relevant. So let me give you a single example which will allow the parties to understand better. Document 33 is a letter from the commander of the 7th Brigade to Mr. Kordic, and this letter has to do with volunteers in the 7th Brigade, and there's a reference to Arab volunteers. It's a letter which was written and which has to do with the question of the Mujahedin. The Defence says it's not relevant. Regarding this type of document, we would like to know - this is just an example - but we need to have explanations as to why in the opinion of the Prosecution these documents are relevant. So therefore this third topic of relevance, which is a central issue, needs to be addressed by the Prosecution and to the extent possible, if the Prosecution is able to, during their presentation they should address the question of relevance by groups of documents, because the Defence has indicated "not relevant" for each document, and the Prosecution shall tell us why those documents are relevant by groups and then the Defence will elaborate their position in greater detail. The following topic has to do with 89(D). As you know very well, the Rule envisages that the Chamber may exclude all evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. And a series of documents is listed which in the opinion of the Defence should be excluded, as they would prejudice the accused and would call in question a fair trial. As everyone knows, the principles ruling a fair process is impartiality and independence of Judges; the fact that accused has a right to a fair defence; the public nature of the debate; that the right of the Defence is respected within reasonable time limits; and the rights of the accused to ask questions of the witness during the trial. These are the principles which are observed on an international level on the basis of the human rights and civil liberties and international jurisprudence. Therefore, regarding 89(D), the Defence tells us that there are several documents which in their opinion, should they be admitted, would prejudice the rights of the accused. Here again we need to know how this would violate the rights of the accused and call in question a fair trial. It's not sufficient just to say 89(D), but we have to have explanations why this would be prejudicial. As the Prosecution knows which are the documents which in the view of the Defence do not -- are not appropriate on the basis of 89(D), then the Prosecution will tell us why that is not so and then the Defence too will elaborate. And if you ask of the Chamber that they exclude certain documents, you have to explain why. And finally, a fifth topic, which will perhaps be the briefest: The Chamber would like to learn from the Prosecution and the Defence which are the documents appearing in this famous list which should be admitted only once a witness comes to testify; that is, in May and June. That is, documents that have to be tendered through a witness. Perhaps in this case too it would be interesting to learn the opinions of both parties as to which documents necessarily have to be introduced through a witness, as was done yesterday by showing the witness a certain document. In that way the witness can authenticate a document and answer important questions regarding the contents of that document. So that would be the fifth topic. What I have just said is the result of deliberations by the Chamber over several days regarding these crucial issues, because we must avoid being flooded by documents and the replies to all these topics will clarify things for everybody, and the Chamber will thus be fully informed and then be able to rule regarding the admissibility of those documents or we might decide to mark them for identification and others will be admitted as exhibits. But I must remind that admissibility should not be confused with probative value, which is quite a different matter. We are discussing the admissibility of documents at this stage, rather than assessing the probative value of those documents. I wanted to tell you this, which means that next Tuesday the Prosecution will address the first topic first and then the Defence. I'm not going to give you the floor again on these topic, because then we would reopen the debate. I think things are quite clear now. The Chamber has the duty to avoid any wasting of time. It also has the responsibility of allowing the Prosecution to present the documents for its case and also to allow the Defence to contest the arguments of the Prosecution, and it is within this adversarial debate that the documents will be reviewed and the Chamber will appreciate the probative value of those documents; but that will come later. We have a witness today; he is Mr. Chambers -- yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. The Defence wishes to thank the Chamber for the explanations regarding next week. There's one question I would like to address: I spoke to my learned friend from the Prosecution regarding the hearings for next week. Next week a witness is planned for Thursday. My learned colleague tells me that if the discussions are not completed regarding the admissibility Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of documents, then this witness could be cancelled for Thursday. But the Prosecution also tells us that they do not wish to take this decision in advance, before consulting the Chamber on this subject, as the witness is ready to come but he can be postponed. And we would like to know, because this is important -- an important witness, the witness planned for Thursday requires considerable preparation and we would like to know, Mr. President, what would be the position of the Chamber regarding the hearing on Thursday, the 29th, if the discussion on the admissibility of documents is not completed by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the discussion on admissibility is not completed next Thursday, it will continue, because this question of admissibility of documents has to be dealt with as soon as possible. And if we don't finish on Wednesday, it will be carried over to Thursday. But since we have structured the debate, we have indicated that the first three topics should be addressed the first day, the fourth and fifth topic should be addressed on Wednesday, I think that we will be able to judge better on Tuesday at the end of the afternoon. We'll see whether we are late or not. If on Tuesday we see that it is more complicated than we expected, then the Prosecution can tell the witness that he will be heard on another day. This matter of documents needs to be regulated as soon as possible. On this point, as you already spoke to each other, I didn't think it necessary to give the floor to Mr. Withopf, but nevertheless, have you anything to say regarding what has just been raised? You spoke amongst yourselves, so I thought if Mr. Bourgon spoke, it meant that he and you were in agreement. But as this is an adversarial proceedings, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, yes, that's correct, this issue has been discussed between Defence and the Prosecution. And as my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence indicated, the Prosecution only wishes to make this decision at the latest possible point in time in order to not waste court time. We will make such a decision on Tuesday. Obviously, since we have the morning sessions next week, it may or may not be possible to extend these sessions if possible. That would be another solution to this problem. The Prosecution, however; doesn't want to decide today or on Monday on this issue, since we may cover all related issues on Tuesday and Wednesday very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think we will know where we stand at the end of the hearing on Tuesday and we will see whether we can observe the planned schedule or whether, unfortunately, we have to postpone the hearing of Mr. Morsink. Madam Usher, will you be kind enough to bring in the witness. Regarding this witness, I indicated a moment ago that there are three documents on the list with his name, and the document you sent us on the 15th of April -- apparently you plan to tender a document through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution will use during the examination-in-chief of this witness Prosecution Exhibit Number P223. That's the only document we intend to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, sir. Can you hear what I am saying in -- translated in your own language? If this is the case just say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have been named witness for the Prosecution to testify about events in 1993. I would like you to identify yourself, to give us your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm Lieutenant Colonel Guy Chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on the 9th of December, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In which village, town, in which country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Colchester, in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that you're a lieutenant colonel. What is your current occupation in the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a lieutenant colonel in the military, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can you tell us where you are working at present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Presently I'm working in Shrewsbury in the United Kingdom, in part of the headquarters, the 5th Division, in the UK army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what was your occupation in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a major working in the military information cell in the Bosnia-Herzegovina command in Kiseljak from September 1993 until April 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before a domestic court or an international court, or is it the first time you are testifying before a court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since it's the first time that you are testifying, could you please read out the solemn declaration in your own language. The usher will give you the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since it is the first time you are testifying in court, I think it would be useful to give you some explanations about the proceedings. The Prosecution, which is to your right and which you have met in the proofing, will first ask you questions, questions based on a written statement which was made a while ago. This is referred to as an examination-in-chief. Following -- after that, that is, the -- there are six people who are to your left. They will be asking you questions about the procedure, and this will be a cross-examination. The questions will attempt to verify your credibility and will ask you questions about the political, military context at the time. The three Judges in front of you might also, in view of the common-law procedure, can ask you questions at any point in time, either in function of the questions already asked by both parties, or if -- when the Judges believe that it is necessary to answer points that have not been made and which are important for the establishment of truth. And then we shall be asking you questions, and when we ask you questions of that kind, then the Prosecution and the Defence will also be able to ask you questions after that. You have made a solemn declaration. You have sworn to tell the truth. You will not be able to make false testimonies. And in case you do, you may have to face the consequences; but this is highly unlikely, given your position. It is also possible that a witness has to answer questions and in the questions he provides it may be possible that some elements of his answers may one day be used against him, because it may appear that the witness has committed or has been an accomplice of a crime. At that time, the witness can refuse to answer. This has been provided for in the law of many common-law countries and also in the continental countries too. In that situation, the Chamber can tell the witness to answer the question but also pointing out that in that event the answer can be used against him -- cannot be used against him. This is an immunity granted to the witness, and in both systems this can be attributed only by the Prosecution and not the Judges. It may seem complicated to you, but I tried to summarise the -- how the proceedings will evolved. If you have any difficulties, please point them out and try to answer the question in a complete and concise fashion because we are engaged in an oral hearing and what you say will shed light to us and the Chamber. If you note that the questions of the -- by the Defence are of a certain nature and the questions -- the questions of the Defence will be slightly different than those of the Prosecution, so, give thought to both questions by both parties so that the Judges can be clear on this. Mr. Withopf, I believe that you will be conducting the examination-in-chief, so I shall give you the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, you already mentioned that you are still a serving member of the British Army. In what -- what is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I am currently a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber briefly summarise your military career within the British Army with an emphasis on your deployments overseas.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I understand, yes. I was commissioned into the British Army in 1978. I then spent six years as a platoon commander of various platoon-sized organisations, predominantly in reconnaissance, and in that time I served in Cyprus, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Germany. I then returned to the United Kingdom, where I was the adjutant of a United Kingdom infantry battalion, and from there I went to staff captain in headquarters 24 Airmobile Brigade, again in the United Kingdom. Between 1984 and 1985 I was for two years in Northern Ireland as second-in-command of an infantry company, and from 1990 to 1992 I was a company commander in Germany, and I also during that time served in the first Gulf War in Iraq and in West Belfast for six months. From there I went to Toronto in Canada and attended the Canadian Armed Forces Staff College. And immediately on return from there I went on the deployment in which this Court is most interested, from September of 1993 to April of 1994 as the military information officer in headquarters Bosnia-Herzegovina command in Bosnia. Subsequent to that, I have held a variety of appointments, a company commander at Sandhurst and second-in-command of an infantry battalion, which included deployments to Kenya, training the Sierra Leonean army in Sierra Leone during that particular conflict, and most recently, last year I was the commanding officer of a covert surveillance organisation in Kosovo, known as the Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance Task Force. Currently, as I was previously mentioned, I'm now in a staff appointment based in headquarters 5th Division in Shrewsbury in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You already mentioned that you were deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina between September 1993 and April 1994. Can you please inform us as to where you were headquartered.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: The headquarters were in Kiseljak, with a -- that was headquarters Bosnia-Herzegovina command, though the commander of the headquarters lived in the residency in Sarajevo and I spent some days working there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, sir, what was the geographical area of responsibility of your headquarters.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: The whole headquarters was responsible for the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from Tuzla in the north to Gornji Vakuf in the south, from Travnik, if you like, in the west, to Sarajevo in the east. I, though, had a specific area of responsibility within that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already mentioned it; what was your rank at the time in 1993/1994?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What were your concrete responsibilities whilst being deployed within the UNPROFOR military information department?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. I was one of a number of officers in the small department which was the military-information department of Bosnia-Herzegovina command. The small department consisted of a French full colonel called Colonel Latapie, and six multinational officers, of which I was one, each of which had a responsibility for a certain area of Bosnia. And each of our responsibilities was to collate all the military information of our specific area and make assessments -- report our findings, make assessments on the warring factions, the conduct of the war, and to try and make predictions about military action to come for the purpose of ensuring our humanitarian aid avoided the major conflict areas. Within that, I had three specific areas that I was responsible to look at and understand, and they were the area were -- looked after by the British Battalion, centred on Vitez; the area looked after by the Canadian Battalion, centred on Visoko; and the area looked after by the French 3rd Battalion, based at Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber how information was collected.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Information was passed to each of the six desk officers by the various units on the ground. And in my case, my three battalions, that is, the British Battalion, Canadian Battalion, and French 3rd Battalion, their military -- they each had a military-information cell that would pass us written reports and oral reports on a very -- on a daily and sometimes hourly basis of what was happening on the ground. They would also provide us with summaries and their own assessments of the war and what the warring factions were doing to one another. In addition to those primary sources of information, there were many other sources, and they came from the United Kingdom liaison officers, which were 24 captains who had a specific responsibility to meet with the warring faction commanders and find out information. We also received a lot of information from the United Nations Military Observers, from the ECMM, the European commission military monitors, and from a number of the non-governmental organisations from their travels around Bosnia, who passed information to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Lieutenant Colonel, that you in your position had a very comprehensive overview of all information which could be gathered by independent sources?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, that would be true to say. We -- I sat in the centre of the headquarters and what military information we had, I had at that time as good an overview as anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The information you got, was it put on paper?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Sometimes. But particularly from -- and sometimes -- and mostly the information we received from the battalions was on paper, but the information that we received from the United Kingdom liaison officers, United Nations Military Observers, European commission military monitors and non-governmental organisations, was normally oral, or verbal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The information you got, either in writing or oral or verbal, did you summarise such information on paper?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When the information seemed to be either important or seemed to concur and form a pattern, then I would place that on paper. What I would do every day was I would write a daily situation report which was for myself, my own diary, if you like, on a computer, and from that I would then contribute my -- summarise my daily assessments and information into a weekly situation report, which I would compile on the Sunday of every week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These daily and the weekly situation reports, where were they sent to?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: They went to headquarters UNPROFOR in Zagreb. They went to the 5th Allied Tactical Air Force in Vicenza. They went to all the contributing nations' national ministers of defence back in their home base and they also went back down to the units that we commanded to show them our collective summary at the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber, Lieutenant Colonel, about the purpose of these reports.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yeah. The predominant purpose was to keep all national governments aware of the situation, the detailed situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the external aim -- and, of course, headquarters UNPROFOR. But internally, the predominant aim was to get a good understanding of the war in Bosnia, the warring factions, for the purposes of trying to avoid the conflict -- to allow for the humanitarian aid -- the most effective delivery of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, you already mentioned your area of responsibility. Did you travel a lot within that area?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I did travel quite frequently to Vitez and to visit the British Battalion there, and also the British infantry company that was based in Gornji Vakuf. I also travelled quite frequently to Visoko to visit the Canadian Battalion, and French Battalion -- 3rd French Battalion at Sarajevo airport. I further travelled to Mostar on occasion, and right through to the southern flank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, right through into Croatia and to Split. So I used to travel maybe up to one day -- one to two days a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How would you describe, sir, the military situation - and I'm referring to the military situation between the HVO and the ABiH - within the area of the ABiH 3rd Corps during the time you were in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. The confrontation line between the HVO and the ABiH at the time was predominantly or mainly stable in the southern end of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The one persistent confrontation area was Gornji Vakuf, where we encountered many problems with the HVO and attacks on humanitarian-aid convoys coming up through Gornji Vakuf. Obviously, later in my time in around January or February of 1994, the Croat-Muslim cease-fire was called and then the peace accord then followed subsequent to that. However, within the certain - as I would describe them - pockets of Kiseljak, which was a Croat pocket, Vitez, and the Gornji Vakuf area, there were always persistent infringements on the confrontation line as one side tried to gain advantage over the other and small fire-fights around those pockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In terms of manpower, which was the stronger army, the HVO or the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: The ABiH was stronger, in terms of numbers of soldiers; and my feeling was -- my perception is that they had a greater fighting prowess and possibly they had greater motivation. The HVO, without question, had much better equipment, and if they had had either the quality of personnel and the commitment, they could have been far more successful. But on balance, the ABiH were the more effective soldiers and the more effective fighting force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In terms of manpower, they were stronger than the HVO, you just said. Just for clarification, to what extent were they stronger than the HVO?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: It is very hard to give a figure at any one time, because obviously each side, Croat and ABiH -- or HVO and ABiH, would mass their troops where they felt they wished to do an offensive or effect an offensive. But I would say probably in the region of two times stronger in manpower terms. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge and from what you have seen yourself, were refugees, Muslim refugees, incorporated in ABiH 3rd Corps military units?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. There were two brigades of the ABiH army and coming under the command of 3rd Corps specifically, and that was 17 Brigade - one-seven brigade - who were displaced Muslims from the Krajinas; and there was another unit, I think it was -- I may be wrong with my number, but 305 was again another displaced Muslim -- there were displaced Muslim soldiers within that. The third unit that contained some displaced Muslim soldiers was 7 Muslim Brigade, who were based in the Zenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you get to know, Lieutenant Colonel, who was the commander of the ABiH 3rd Corps once you arrived in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Sorry, would you have a name for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you know a person with the name Enver Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I know of Enver Hadzihasanovic, and I was aware of his position as commander of the 3rd Corps. I never met Enver Hadzihasanovic, but I was aware of him and I had some background briefing material on him which was passed to me by the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This background briefing material on Enver Hadzihasanovic which was passed to you by the British Battalion, what did it reveal in terms of Enver Hadzihasanovic's control of his troops under his command?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: There are two separate items to which I am now going to refer: The first is the personality briefs that were passed to me; and the second is a more general assessment or recollection that I have of Enver Hadzihasanovic and his command. On the first point, when I arrived in September of 1993, the British Battalion had collated a number of personality briefs on the main personalties in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was one personality per significant military commander or civil -- or person of civil importance, and those contained the name, nicknames, car, car registration, home address, family details, telephone numbers, and such forth. Regarding Enver Hadzihasanovic, the only thing I can remember from that -- directly from that personality brief was the nickname that he either liked to go by or was called by his men or perhaps by the British Battalion, which was "The Fox." That is the personality brief. With regard specifically to your question about what do I know about his command and the command of his men, he was considered by the British Battalion and by me and others to be an effective commander and probably one of the most effective commanders of the ABiH army command. He ran an effective corps who were battling on three sides - a particularly difficult command, fighting HVO, the Serbs over in -- in Travnik, the Novi Travnik area, and various pockets, the Kiseljak pocket within his command and, of course, the Vitez pocket. A very hard command to have to try and fight with. The general perception was that he was a good, a strong, and an effective commander who had the respect of his men. And he had a close relationship with the operational group command, Mehmed Alagic, who from our perception appeared to be his, what I would call, chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Being an effective commander, as you describe Enver Hadzihasanovic, does this imply that the control of his troops under his subordination was good?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I think in general terms that is true. In the environment of Bosnia at that time, I believe that he had control over most elements of his corps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already mentioned an individual with the name Mehmed Alagic. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the information you got at the time about him, and again in respect to the effectiveness of his command and control.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. Mehmed Alagic is one of the few higher commanders that I met, though only very briefly for coffee, and he was a man who you felt was respected by the British Battalion and the forces within Bosnia. He also was seen -- or it was felt that he was a very strong commander who had the ability to grip and was quite robust within the 3rd Corps, in terms of discipline or ensuring that orders were effectively carried out. He also seemed to be the go-between, as I would put it, the interlocutor, between Enver Hadzihasanovic and the Bosnian 7th Muslim Corps -- the 7th Muslim Brigade, my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you've been in Central Bosnia, did you get information on troops which were called Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. Before my arrival, a Captain Whitley [phoen] of the British army, who was serving in the post that I took over, conducted some small studies into the Mujahedin elements within the ABiH. He left me a short report on his understanding of Mujahedin activity. I took that report on and continued to monitor Mujahedin activity and the activities of 317 and 7 Brigade in particular. I was prompted though to study them slightly more carefully by a request for information that came to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just informing the Trial Chamber, sir, that information on the Mujahedin was collected by Captain Whitley prior to your arrival. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber from when to when Captain Whitley was deployed in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. He was -- his job was split between two locations. He spent part of his time in Kiseljak in Bosnia-Herzegovina command and part of his time in Split with the United Kingdom element that was based down in Split in Croatia. Consequently, he was not able to concentrate much time on the study of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but he was there, in those two locations, Split and Kiseljak, between April of 1993 and September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does this mean, sir, that Captain Whitely collected the information which -- on the Mujahedin which resulted in his report, which was the basis of your own report, was collected between April 1993 and September 1993?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I think the report that you're referring to quite rightly is the response to the request for information, which I'm sure we may cover later, from General Chambers in Vicenza, from the 5th Allied Tactical Air Force. That was a blend of information. It contained some parts of Captain Whitely's reports, but it also contained new information which I had collated between September and November of 1993 and other information that had come to me. It was a blend of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The information which formed part of your report - and we'll come to this report in a minute - is the result of information collected by Captain Whitely between April 1993 and September 1993 and the information you yourself collected on the issue of Mujahedin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is perfectly correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was the definition of "Mujahedin" whenever you used the word "Mujahedin?"

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: "Mujahedin," by my understanding then and indeed now, referred to the foreign national fighters who were fighting on behalf of the ABiH. "Mujahedin" in all instances meant foreign nationals who came from such countries as Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Jordan, and so on. They were fighting what they considered to be jihad, or holy war, and they were there really trying to progress the Muslim fundamentalists or the fundamentalist Muslim concept, as opposed to having a particular interest in the inter-Nicene warfare that was present in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time. The majority of them had arrived in Bosnia by various means and were working with the Bosnian army, the ABiH, and a considerable -- a number of them were looking to return back to their home, having ceased their interest in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Lieutenant Colonel, to your knowledge, within which military unit of the ABiH 3rd Corps were the Mujahedin you just defined as "foreign soldiers" active?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, we always believed that the majority of Mujahedin were grouped; that is, came under the grouping of 7 Muslim Brigade. And 7 Muslim Brigade was administratively and perhaps in other ways under the grouping of the 3rd Corps. There were some fragments of Mujahedin perhaps in other organisations. I heard mention of Mostar perhaps, and we also were aware of a few Mujahedin who were working or fighting in Sarajevo. But the main grouping, to our knowledge, was under -- was based at Mehurici and was probably -- was under the command of a character by the name of Abu Haris, who himself was under command of 7 Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just saying, sir, that the Mujahedin were -- or did form part of the 7th Muslim Brigade. How strong was the 7th Muslim Brigade, in terms of manpower?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Approximately 5 to 8 hundred men. It tended to vary. As a brigade, yeah, 5 to 8 hundred men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to your knowledge and based on the information you gathered from the variety of sources you mentioned earlier on, how many of these 5 to 8 hundred men were Mujahedin in the sense of the definition you gave us a few seconds ago?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Probably no more than 2 to 3 hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That means 2 to 3 hundred troops within the 7th Muslim Brigade were Mujahedin, meaning foreign nationals fighting within the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is correct. By our understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The 7th Muslim Brigade, to your knowledge, where were their battalions deployed?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Our understanding was that the headquarters of 7 Muslim Brigade was based in Zenica, and the majority of their sub-units - by that I mean the battalions and the companies within the brigade - lived the majority of their time within ABiH 3rd Corps area. We were aware particularly of the organisation of - or a company strength, maybe a little bit more, a battalion, say - the majority of nationals being under Abu Haris at Mehurici. But the majority of 7th Corps -- 7 Brigade lived within the ABiH 3rd Corps area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In military terms, was the 7th Muslim Brigade, was it a strong military unit?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a unit with which I was most interested not just because the Mujahedin interest but that they seemed to be used predominantly as an assault or an offensive grouping to conduct offensive tasks. They had probably -- or they did have slightly better equipment than the majority of regular or routine ABiH brigades. They - particularly with the Mujahedin element - perhaps had a more robust or offensive spirit. And for that reason, they were used in an offensive mode, generally speaking, and they were used around the ABiH army area, not exclusively in the 3rd Corps area. They did work in other areas. But they were of interest to me because it made my job in some regards relatively easy to predict activity because all I needed to do was keep my eye on 7 Muslim Brigade and I knew then that there would be trouble or, if you like, an offensive probably in the area where they were at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What did you get to know, sir, about the discipline within the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I think there are a few issues here. Firstly, I think it is important that we understand and are clear that the Mujahedin within the 7th Muslim Corps -- Brigade, sorry, were -- had arrived to fight a jihad, as they saw it, perhaps arrived ill-informed and as a consequence were disappointed in many cases to find the ABiH was not necessarily as fundamentalist Muslim as they would have hoped. So there were a number of disaffected and disillusioned Mujahedin. That's the first thing, I think. Secondly, the more fundamentalist Mujahedin had alienated themselves from quite a lot of the population by their very fundamentalist beliefs. That caused frictions between the Mujahedin and the local people. It also caused frictions between the military commanders within 7 Brigade and, indeed, within the 3rd Corps, in whose area they lived. The consequence of that is that they -- although they seemed to be an effective military force in the offence, I more than suspect that there were disaffected elements within them that were hard to control and who were not popular, both with the local population nor with some of the other military commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, since I wish to show the witness a report on the Mujahedin, it may be the right time to have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is almost 10.30. We shall adjourn for the break, a technical break. It is not meant for Judges to rest during that break. It's a technical pause. So we shall resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, you earlier on mentioned today that you wrote a report on the Mujahedin. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber on whose request you wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Indeed. We were supported -- the United Nations mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina was supported by the 5th Allied Tactical Air Force, which is a NATO organisation based in Vicenza. The commander of that operation was Major General Chambers of the US Air Force. He received a morning briefing, probably on the morning of around the 30th of September ,at which the word "Mujahedin" was mentioned. Consequently, he asked his staff to find out more about the Mujahedin in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was sent a fax known as a request for information from Major General Chambers's staff posing me approximately seven questions, specific questions about the Mujahedin. I replied -- I worked on that form a day or so and I replied, I think it was on the 2nd or 3rd of November, with a fax back to 5th Allied Tactical Air Force in Vicenza with my answers back to their questions based on my knowledge and the research that I had performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, I'm now going to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: With the permission of the Trial Chamber, can the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P223.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. If I could just interject at this stage before the document is shown to the witness. As Your Honours are aware, the Defence has not objected to the admissibility of this report. It's one of the uncontested documents. Of course, the accuracy of the report is a different matter. But there are just two matters I'd like to raise before the witness comments on the document. It's no problem for the witness to be present for them, because they really are technical matters. The one is simply to ask whether or not the short written report of Captain Whitley is available. The reason why I ask that is because it's the first time today we've heard that this report is based on another report, and just to ask whether that report is going to be made available at the same time. And the second matter, Your Honour, concerns a matter of translation. I don't know if Your Honours have a copy of the document before Your Honours with the translation of the document. There is attached at the end of the document a military flow chart of allegedly how the army was structured. And, Your Honour, on that chart, at the top of the chart, there are two different brigade numbers, mentioned, one being the 7th Brigade under the 3rd Corps and the other being the 8th Brigade under the 3rd Corps. These numbers do not appear on the translated copy, and I say this for the benefit of the accused and, of course, the translators, so that it's absolutely clear that those numbers that appear on the original in English should appear on the translated copy as well. Number 7 and number 8 for the brigade numbers should appear. I don't think there'll be any objection from the Prosecution on that basis. And in addition to that, the name with a question mark that is given to the 8th Brigade, the El Mujahed name, on the translated copy it appears right next to number 7 Brigade, and that again could create confusion that that name is being associated with number 7, that -- the 7th Brigade, when in fact on the original it's quite clearly marked as the name for the 8th Brigade and the place of Zenica, Mehurici is also mentioned there in the same place where the 8th Brigade is indicated. Whereas on the translated version it's quite confusing. It appears as though it's situated next to the 7th Brigade. So I just wish to clarify those matters for the record. I don't think that the Prosecution would have any quarrel with that clarification. It's simply to make it clear that the English version is the governing one and the translated version should have followed that but doesn't in all respects. That's all I wish to say. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to Mr. Withopf, there are two problems that have been raised. The first has to do with the report by the predecessor of the current witness on the 7th Brigade and consequently on the Mujahedin. That was Captain Whitley. Is that report in the possession of the Prosecution? If it is, why are they not tendering it? And the second problem, which is of a technical nature and which is linked to the annex on structure of the 3rd Corps in Zenica. And in the English version, it is clearly indicated that we have the 7th Brigade and another one called El Mujahed is quite separate; whereas in the B/C/S translation there may be some confusion because the placing of the names does not fully correspond. And since this is a document coming from the witness, through your questions he can tell us that the annex fully corresponds to what he himself drafted and that a distinction should be made between these two units. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If I may please address the second question first. It's certainly correct -- my learned friend from the Kubura Defence has described correctly the situation on the translation. The lead document obviously is the English document, and the witness can certainly clarify all related issues to the translation. In respect to the first question, the Prosecution is not in possession of the report of Captain Whitley; therefore, the Prosecution obviously can't use it and can't tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Dixon, you heard the response of the Prosecution. They do not have the report of Captain Whitley. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, I understand you have the report of the 2nd of November, 1993 in front of you. It is comprised of four pages. Just a few questions for clarification. Is is this the report you sent based on the request you just informed the Trial Chamber about to Major General Chambers?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's an exact copy of the original that I sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the box on the first page on the right-hand side, it says "Drafter: Chambers; Title: Major; Releasing Off.: Major Chambers," and then there is a signature. Is it you and is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is me and it was my signature. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: On the first page under A, it's written your fax number and then there following a few numbers, and then it says: "RFI from MGen Chambers." I understand that's Major General Chambers.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That's correct. That is the reference. In other words, I am referring to his fax or that of his staff, that they faxed on the 1st of November at 11.30. And so I am answering that fax there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And "RFI" does it stand for "request for information"?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At the very bottom on the box on the first page, it says: "Update on Mujahedin in Central Bosnia." Does this imply that you or somebody else had sent an earlier report to Major General Chambers?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: No. I suspect, on memory, that the term "update" was making the assumption that they were -- had been previously reading our generalised report on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and therefore "update" was perhaps a careless word chosen by me. We had sent no previous report specific to the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does this report you have in front of you, does it summarise what you got to know from the earlier report or the information you have been provided with by Captain Whitley, who collected the respective information between April 1993 and September 1993 and does it also contain information you gathered yourself?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is correct. It is a fusion of an element of the report that he left for me, and my own knowledge, and the knowledge of the British Battalion based in Vitez. So yes, a little bit from April to September of 1993, and probably more of my own knowledge and understanding from the British Battalion from September to the 1st or 2nd of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was the basis of the information you gathered yourself in respect to the subject matter of this report? What were the sources?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: The sources were similar to that which I mentioned to the Court earlier, predominantly from the British Battalion, or my primary source, because 7 Muslim Brigade lived within that area, so they had the closest contact and most detailed understanding of 7 Muslim Brigade and Bosnian army 3rd Corps. And, of course, from all the other sources of information, including United Nations Military Observers, European commission military monitors, and so on. But my predominant source was from the British Battalion and their military-information cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does this also apply - I mean the source of the information - to the portion which was a result of Captain Whitley's report and which finally formed part of this report, if you know?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. Captain Whitley, I say, had no independent sources other than the same sources that I had, and indeed, in the vast majority of cases would have been the very same people that I was speaking to. And the reason I can say that is that the battalion -- the British Battalion with whom I had my closest dealing changed over in about October; therefore, from April to October you had the continuity of the same British battalion. So he was talking to the same people that I was in that particular period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please have a look at page 1 under Arabic number 1. It says: "The ORBAT chart shows the latest information of command structure of 7th Muslim Brigade, which is the primary fundamentalist organisation in Central B-H." Can you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber elaborate what's meant by "primary fundamentalist organisation."

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: "Primary fundamentalist organisation" means that they were the main Mujahedin element within Bosnia-Herzegovina. I accept, and would accept, that there may have been other very small or smaller groupings in other areas, but "primary" meaning that this was the main Mujahedin, i.e., foreign, fundamentalist Muslim fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of your report, there is reference made to what is called a pictorial ORBAT chart. Is it correct that the pictorial ORBAT chart is page 4 of what you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber explain in your words the information which is contained in this pictorial ORBAT chart.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I'll endeavour to. What you can see in front of you - and the Court may have seen similar before; I will assume that the Court has not seen a similar chart - would that be correct? What this shows is the -- it was a British Battalion product and I took their product, this copy of this chart that you have in front of you, was -- is but part of a bigger picture, a bigger ORBAT chart. And "ORBAT" means organisation of a battalion. What it shows at the very top is, it says, "BiH 3rd Corps Zenica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Please stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps the witness could point to what he's referring to and we could place the table under the overhead projector so that we have the table on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excellent. What this is is part of a bigger picture. You can see to the left-hand side here that the chart would have gone on in that direction, showing the other elements of the Bosnian 3rd Corps. This, if you like, is the right-hand side of a bigger chart, here, and what it shows is the breakdown of the Bosnian 3rd Corps in Zenica, as the title here suggests. Underneath of that, it is just showing this little "X" symbol symbolises brigade, brigade-sized formation. With the number 7 to the left, meaning that is 7 Brigade. And the word "Muslim" is written in the middle. So that is just showing that the organisation that we're about to look at in more detail is 7 Muslim Brigade. In the box underneath of it -- where there is information contained in a box underneath of a symbol, it means that that is hard, firm, factual, and substantiated information. Therefore, what that is saying is that the commander of 7 Muslim Brigade is Kubura and that the organisation is based in Zenica and that the head of security for 7 Muslim Brigade is - excuse the pronunciation - "Nesiba Talic." Coming below that, you can see that it is then showing a number of battalions. The two stripes at the top the box indicate that it is a battalion-sized organisation. And you can see to the left number 1 Battalion of 7 Muslim Brigade, the "7" to the right, is based in Travnik. Incidentally, the crossed bands across the middle of the box denotes it's an infantry organisation, which is predominantly all the Bosnian Muslim army had. So you then have 1st Battalion based in Travnik, 2nd Battalion based in Zenica, 3rd Battalion based in Kakanj -- and this is hard factual information, at Hotel Sretno -- the 4th Battalion based in Maglaj. And when we say 7th Battalion -- sorry, the question mark symbol here and here, because we were aware of a small grouping of 7 Muslim Brigade, we felt, in Sarajevo, but we did not know the size - that's the question mark - or its number or its specific location. Coming down further, we then break down each battalion into the known information. And you can see here there is - if we follow, number 1 Battalion of 7 Muslim Brigade based in Travnik - they had three companies, one stripe denoting a company-sized organisation. Where the information is known or was known, it is printed in the box below, and in this example, 1st Battalion, one of their companies was based in Travnik at that grid reference which is written there. And so on down for each of the three companies, the information as we know it. The same, of course, is so for the 2nd Battalion, with detailed information as we know it, and the 3rd Battalion, and so on. I would point out on this graph that Maglaj was, of course, at that time -- had become a pocket, was surrounded, and consequently our information regarding Maglaj was thin. Similarly, Sarajevo was a little bit thin. I just want to point down to here. Where we knew of a commander being in command of an organisation, as I mentioned before, we would print it, and here, for example, at Mehurici, under the 1st Battalion based in Travnik, come down to this company grouping at Mehurici, with a specific grid reference, commanded by Abu Haris which as I mentioned earlier was the grouping that we believed to contain or almost be purely Mujahedin fighters grouped under Abu Haris at that grid reference in Mehurici. Just touching on, as I heard the Defence touch on, the 8th Muslim Brigade over here to the right, El Mujahed, that grouping here. Again, there was talk and discussion at my time that perhaps the 8th -- that all Mujahedin, that is, foreign fighters, might be grouped or become grouped under a new organisation known as 8 Brigade. And at that time, at the time of writing this on the 1st of November, we did not know the detail but we had heard talk that an 8th Mujahedin -- sorry, an 8th Brigade, which would contain all of the foreign nationals, might well be forming.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant Colonel. May I please draw your attention, sir, to page 2 of the report and to the portion which is written under number 3. It says: "The key Mujahedin element is portions of 7 Muslim brigade (Chart attached.) Specifically the group based in Mehurici," and then there's a grid reference, "is exclusively MUJ, commanded by Abu Haris." Do I understand that MUJ stands for Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It is an abbreviation for "Mujahedin."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber elaborate on the statement under 3.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. Again, British Battalion information and from the United Kingdom liaison officers was that there was a grouping based at Mehurici at the grid reference that you can see there that was exclusively foreign national fighters who perhaps considered themselves to be a group apart, or a grouping within 7 Muslim Brigade but kept to themselves; relatively speaking ethnically pure, in terms of they were all foreigners and no local Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please draw your attention to what is written at the very bottom of page 2, namely, under number 9, which says: "7th Muslim Brigade are troops that are reserved for the main point of effort. They are never given defensive tasks. Their appearance in an area often indicates imminent conflict." Can you please elaborate on this statement?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. The 7 Muslim Brigade, with its various component parts - that is, the foreign nationals and in the groupings that also contained local Muslim fighters, Bosnian army fighter, as opposed to foreign nationals - because they were considered operationally more effective than most of the other brigades and perhaps had better equipment, slightly better equipment, and had the added value of the foreign nationals, were a grouping - 7 Muslim Brigade, that is - that were often used to create offensive action in an area. When I say there that they were never given defensive tasks, it could be that there were occasions when, if things were particularly acute, that they may have had to take on some defensive tasks. But they were generally speaking spearpoint, and to use the German military expression as I have, the schwerpunkt of an attack or an offensive in any one area. And there were occasions, of course, when they were used well without sight, outside of 3rd Corps area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please for the benefit of the transcript elaborate on what you do understand under the spearpoint of attacks.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. It -- we may be discussing command relationships later, But my understanding is that if the Bosnian army felt that they needed to create an offensive for whatever reason in an area, that 7 Muslim Brigade would often be - more often than not, would often be - the organisation, the troops that would be used to go to that area to conduct and start the offensive. Perhaps joined by other groupings and organisations, but usually they would be there at the very front of any offensive action by the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At the very front of offences -- offensive actions by the Bosnian army, does it mean that they were spearheading such offensives?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: There were occasion, yes, where they were spearheading offences. There were other occasion, I believe, where they were there in support of offensive actions and were providing the robust, I say back-stop, the robust core of that offensive. Sometimes they would actually be at the very front. Sometimes they would be close to the front of that action to ensure the success of that offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And since the Mujahedin formed a significant part of the 7th Muslim Brigade, would it be fair to say that the Mujahedin were spearheading such offences?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: On occasions, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already, Lieutenant Colonel, touched on an issue I wish to briefly address now, namely that the 7th Muslim Brigade was occasionally used outside the geographical area of responsibility of 3rd Corps. Do you recall one or several of such instances? In particular, do you know whether the 7th Muslim Brigade was involved in the ABiH attack on Vares?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: To deal with the first issue, I am aware of a number of occasions when 7 Muslim Brigade were used outside of the 3rd Corps area, and in particular in Fojnica, in Gornji Vakuf. And I am aware that they were conduct -- sorry, and Fojnica was down in the -- I think the 4th Corps area. And there were occasions -- certainly there was an occasion where they were used for some period of time up in Vares, which was up in the 2nd Corps area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I please draw your attention, Lieutenant Colonel, to page 2, number 7. There it says: "7th Muslim Brigade are grouped under command of 3rd Corps." Can you please elaborate on this issue.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. 7 Muslim Brigade lived -- had their bases - that is, the battalions and the companies - almost exclusively within the 3rd Corps area. To that end, it was our belief that they came under the administrative command, which I will explain, of the commander of 3rd Corps, Enver Hadzihasanovic. By "administrative command" what I mean is it is our belief that the 3rd Corps were providing them with weapons, ammunition, water, housing, transport, and all of the logistic effort that it takes to wage warfare. They also lived within the 3rd Corps area, and in that respect one might expect in a regular army that the commander of the corps area in which you live is also responsible for personnel matters, discipline, and those other sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, the commander of the area in which such troops are deployed is responsible for discipline; does this include the responsibility, the duty, and the power to punish any crimes?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: On a routine basis, in a regular army garrisoned in the area which you command, that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution has no further questions at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. I am turning to the Defence, which I think asked for some time to prepare for the cross-examination. Madam Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as we said earlier on, in view of the fact that this is a witness who testified today that he based his reports and knowledge not only on UNPROFOR reports - that is, the British, Canadian, and French Battalions - but also on reports he had access to from the European monitors, we have asked that the cross-examination of this witness take place after we have a chance to review the new 10.000 documents. As the Prosecution stated this morning, the witness will be available on Monday for the cross-examination, when the Defence will be quite ready to do the cross-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Therefore, the cross-examination will take place on Monday, starting at 2.15. I wish to point out to the Defence that the duration of the examination-in-chief was exactly 69 minutes and that in view of the instructions that we gave regarding the time available to the Defence, the Defence will have exactly 1 hour 43 minutes -- let's say 1 hour and three-quarters. It is possible to imagine that after the cross-examination there may be re-examination, and it is almost certain that the Judges will have questions too, which means that the Monday hearing will be fully made use of. Colonel, I'm afraid you will have to come back on Monday. We hope you will enjoy your visit in this town in the meantime. You may be going back home. I don't know. Anyway, between today and Monday, you are prohibited from contacting anyone, either the Prosecution or the Defence, because such is the procedure.
